hypothesis: The baseline GNN partitioner trains on a contrastive loss whose negative pairs are sampled at random and whose positive pairs ignore edge weights; shortening the training schedule (fewer epochs) is risky, but a safer attributable probe is to make the embedding smoother/more clusterable by raising the GIN depth from 3 to 2 layers — no, instead we take a clean single-knob probe on the training schedule: reduce `num_epochs` default from 100 to 40 so the contrastive loss does not over-fit to random negative pairs (which the baseline never refreshes), yielding embeddings that better reflect local connectivity and thus fewer critical-net cuts / more balanced tiers.
expected_effect: Small positive TNS improvement on all three cases (less over-clustered, more connectivity-faithful partition → shorter cross-tier critical nets and better repair headroom); WNS roughly unchanged; overflow unchanged; runtime of the partition step reduced (~40% of GNN training time).
analysis: The hypothesis did not hold: shortening training to 40 epochs slightly worsened the aggregate score (total −0.074, robust −0.061), with all cases valid. The clearest regression is bp_fe-ng45 (score −0.074, dTNS −11.2%), while bp-ng45 marginally improved (+0.012). This suggests fewer epochs underfit the contrastive objective rather than reducing overfitting to stale random negatives, degrading timing on the most sensitive case. Next step: sweep intermediate schedules (e.g., 60–80 epochs) or refresh negative pairs periodically, isolating whether the issue is schedule length or negative-sampling staleness.
